issues.item: Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, stranger interaction and dark spaces are hard to link to the trauma context given the rest of the profile. The other nodes center on bodily harm/contamination-type consequences, pain recall, and event-site avoidance; these triggers instead suggest interpersonal or assault-related trauma themes.

Startle to unexpected touch is not impossible, but paired with stranger interaction and the absence of interpersonal threat appraisals, it pulls the profile toward an assault/interpersonal trauma pattern rather than toxic exposure. This makes the threat profile less coherent with the stated trauma type and with the other threat items.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can see what happened just by looking at me implies visible stigma or externally legible damage. With toxic chemical exposure, this could fit only if there were clear visible injuries, but the rest of the profile emphasizes internal bodily reactions, pain recall, and disorganized memory rather than visible disfigurement. Together this item sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, the threat profile is centered on contamination/physical harm cues. 'Flashbacks' is not impossible, but paired with the rest of this profile it implies a strongly re-experiencing, event-reliving presentation. That would usually be linked to trauma-congruent cues about the exposure itself; here the trigger and appraisal content is instead dominated by darkness/night and generalized bodily defectiveness, making this specific threat item clinically hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
issues.explanation: 'Hypervigilance towards people' is a poor fit for a toxic chemical exposure trauma when there are no corresponding interpersonal threat appraisals or memories. The rest of the profile focuses on bodily reactions, event site avoidance, and attempts to suppress the memory, which are coherent for chemical exposure. Vigilance for dangerous people introduces an interpersonal-assault type coping pattern that is not supported by the trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items and is therefore clinically incoherent in this profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' is hard to reconcile as a primary trigger for toxic chemical exposure when the other trigger items are darkness/night-time and the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, environmental threat, and sensory reminders. Positive affect as a trigger is not impossible, but here it is clinically disconnected from the trauma type and from the other selected nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' fits traumas involving visible stigma, assault, or shame-based social exposure better than toxic chemical exposure as represented by the rest of this profile. It does not cohere well with the other appraisals, which are about bodily malfunction and defectiveness rather than visible external marking.

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 26-year-old Colombian-American graduate student who presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after sustaining accidental toxic chemical exposure in a university laboratory. She had been working late into the evening, alone in the research facility, when a storage container of industrial solvent ruptured. The room filled rapidly with fumes in the dark corridor adjacent to the lab - she had stepped out to retrieve equipment when the lights on that wing failed simultaneously - and she spent what she later estimated was nearly twenty minutes disoriented in near-total darkness, unable to locate the exit, her eyes burning, her chest tightening with each breath. By the time emergency responders reached her, she had collapsed. She spent four days in hospital, during which she underwent repeated respiratory assessments, the antiseptic smell of the ward threading itself into every waking hour of her recovery.

In the weeks that followed, Valentina found that the memory of the event resisted the kind of coherent telling that might have made it feel manageable. She knew, in some abstract sense, what had happened - the sequence of events was documented in the incident report - but when she tried to recall it herself, the images came out of order, fragmentary and lurching, and she found herself unable to find the words to describe what it had actually been like. What made this more distressing was that the memory did not stay past-tense: when fragments returned, she felt a tightening across her chest and a burning sensation along her throat, the same physical pain she had experienced during the exposure itself. These somatic intrusions reinforced her growing conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with her - that her body had been damaged in ways that were not fully visible, or that she was constitutionally too fragile to have recovered normally. She had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that there was something defective in her as a person, that other people did not fall apart the way she did.

This sense of bodily betrayal - the feeling that her body was an enemy operating outside her control - fed directly back into how she experienced her own memories. When she tried to recall the event in order to make sense of it, the physical sensations that arose confirmed, to her, that the danger was not truly over. Her body reacting as though she were still in that dark corridor seemed like evidence that she was still, in some meaningful way, there. This meant that the memories themselves became triggers for renewed physical alarm, and the physical alarm in turn made the memories feel more vivid and more disordered, a loop she could not step outside of.

Certain external cues had become unbearable. Darkness - any dark space, including her own bedroom before she reached the light switch - produced immediate physical reactivity: racing heart, shallow breathing, the full-body bracing of a person expecting impact. Waking in the night, disoriented in the dark, reliably produced the most severe episodes. The smell of antiseptic, encountered in a campus health clinic she visited for an unrelated matter, stopped her at the door. These triggers, once established, began to structure her life. Because she had come to believe her body was unreliable and that she herself was somehow defective, she interpreted each triggered response not as a normal trauma reaction but as further proof of her own fragility - and this appraisal made the triggers feel more threatening, more inevitable, and harder to approach.

Valentina responded by building an elaborate architecture of avoidance. She had not returned to the laboratory building since the incident, arranging with her supervisor to conduct all her work remotely - an accommodation that had begun to strain that relationship. She worked to push the memory away whenever it surfaced, trying to erase it rather than process it, which left it unintegrated and prone to intrusion. She kept lights on throughout her apartment at all times. She also scanned her surroundings constantly when in unfamiliar spaces, her body perpetually tensed for the next sign of danger - and this hypervigilance, exhausting as it was, kept her nervous system primed so that even minor stimuli, including an unexpected touch on the shoulder from a classmate, made her react with alarm. The vigilance itself became a source of physiological arousal that made triggers more potent and the sense of threat feel more real.

Valentina sought help after a panic episode in a campus stairwell during a power fluctuation dimmed the lights for less than a minute. She sat on the steps for an hour afterward, unable to move. What frightened her most was not the episode itself but what she believed it meant: that she was getting worse, not better, and that her body could no longer be trusted to tell the difference between memory and reality. What she most hoped for, she said quietly at intake, was to be able to sleep with the lights off again.
